title: What time is it? — quarter past, half past, quarter to
title_target: क्या बजा है? — kyaa bajaa hai?
goal: Tell the time and make appointments — and learn the three little words Hindi uses for quarter past, half past, and quarter to, plus two special words that have no English match.
bekal: ask and say what time it is
name the parts of the day: सुबह, दोपहर, शाम, रात

dialogs.title: संवाद — Making a date
dialogs.intro: Rahul asks Ani to meet tomorrow. In line six Ani discovers something useful: Indonesian and Hindi both use "half", but count from opposite ends — and Hindi counts the English way.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: SaaRhe chhah… you mean six thirty?

notes: **Good news first: साढ़े तीन means 3:30, exactly like English "half past three".** Hindi names the hour that has **already gone by**: साढ़े तीन is literally "three plus a half". Ani is surprised because in Indonesian "half four" means 3:30 — the next hour. ⚠️ If you've learned German or Dutch, beware the same trap: *halb sieben* is 6:30 there, but *साढ़े सात* is 7:30 in Hindi.

**So for an English speaker the logic is already familiar**, and British *half seven* (= 7:30) works exactly like Hindi. Just remember that **the number you hear is the hour that has passed**, and every other marker makes sense.

**Three marker words, each looking in a different direction.** **सवा** = a quarter **past** the number (सवा चार = 4:15). **साढ़े** = half **past** the number (साढ़े चार = 4:30). **पौने** = a quarter **to** the number (पौने चार = 3:45). ⚠️ The first two look forward from the number, the third looks back. When in doubt, use the long way: *चार बजकर पंद्रह मिनट*.

**डेढ़ and ढाई are special words for 1½ and 2½, and you must use them.** There is no *साढ़े एक* or *साढ़े दो* — those forms aren't used at all. **डेढ़ बजे** = 1:30, **ढाई बजे** = 2:30, and only then **साढ़े तीन** = 3:30 and so on. Both words are also used for amounts: *डेढ़ किलो* (1.5 kg), *ढाई घंटे* (2.5 hours).

**बजे means "o'clock", and it comes from a word meaning "to strike" (like a clock chiming).** *चार बजे* = at four o'clock, *चार बजे हैं* = it's four o'clock now. To ask the time now: **क्या बजा है?** To ask the time of a meeting: **कितने बजे?** ⚠️ The two questions are different and often mixed up.

**को after parts of the day, but not after clock times.** *शाम **को*** (in the evening), *सुबह **को*** (in the morning), *रात **को*** — but *छह बजे* without को. For days: *सोमवार **को*** (on Monday). With आज and कल: nothing at all — *आज शाम को*, *कल सुबह*.

**समझ गई — a form you haven't learned yet, but too useful to put off.** *समझ गया* (male) / *समझ गई* (female) means "got it, I understand", and it's what real people say, not *मैं समझती हूँ*, which sounds like a textbook. Its partner: **समझ नहीं आया** (I didn't get it). Unit 13 explains the form; for now learn it whole.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Read the second column aloud while covering the first, then the other way round. Time has to come out fast, not be worked out.

head: Part of the day
हिंदी
Pronunciation
Roughly
rows: day after tomorrow / day before yesterday

after: ⚠️ **कल means "yesterday" AND "tomorrow", and परसों means "the day after tomorrow" AND "the day before yesterday".** The verb form decides: *कल मैं आई* (yesterday I came) vs. *कल मैं आऊँगी* (tomorrow I'll come). It sounds impossible until you realize Hindi sees time as a distance from today, not a direction. Unit 13 comes back to this.

grammars.title: Making appointments
after: ⚠️ **देर** means "lateness" **and** "length of time". *मुझे देर हो गई* = I'm late; *कितनी देर?* = how long? Context tells them apart, and both are very common.

sections.title: Indian time, and how to read an appointment

blocks.text: Something to know before you make your first appointment in India: there's a real difference between formal and social appointments, and both are spoken with the same words.

head: Situation
What usually happens
A helpful sentence
rows: often an hour later than stated

blocks.title: Four sentences to rescue an appointment
items: **मैं थोड़ा लेट हूँ, दस मिनट में पहुँचती हूँ।** — I'm running a bit late, I'll be there in ten minutes.
**आप कहाँ तक पहुँचे?** — Where have you got to?
**कोई बात नहीं।** — No problem. (the answer to an apology; used constantly)
**फिर कभी?** — Some other time? (a gentle way to postpone without refusing — unit 19 says more)

blocks.text: And one small, pleasing note. The word **कल** meaning both yesterday and tomorrow isn't a flaw in the language; it reflects a way of seeing time you'll recognize from everyday English, where "soon" can mean two hours or two months and nobody is confused. Hindi just organizes it more neatly: the **distance** from today is named, and the **direction** is left to the verb. Once you're used to it, it stops feeling strange and starts feeling economical.

क्या बजा है? — साढ़े छह बजे। — मैं नौ बजे तक फ़्री हूँ। — कल शाम को मिलें? — मुझे थोड़ी देर हो रही है। — कोई बात नहीं।
